title: Cole Brothers Circus and the minstrel units under J.C. Miles
summary: White describes the 1918 season with the Cole Brothers Circus, its owners, and the bands of the Virginia, Alabama and Georgia minstrel shows.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: All right. Then I, for my season, 1918, I began that season with the Cole Brothers Circus under the directorship of J.C. Myers, the husband of Lizzie Myers. Contrary to what another publisher said about he being the father, that's not true. That was her husband. George, yeah. And, uh, that's right. And J.C. Myers' minstrel shows on the Cole Brothers Circus was a unit similar to the Georgia Smart Set, the Alabama minstrels, and the Virginia minstrels. The man owned all of those shows. In fact, the Cole Brothers Circus was the second, was the largest circus, but they had another one called the Spock Circus that they had bought also.
I think I've seen the Cole Brothers Circus from the last year.

Then the Jones Brothers and Wilson Circus of 30 Cars. Well, Elmer Jones and Augusta Jones was the owner of all those shows. Three circuses and three outstanding minstrel attractions. And they were fine shows. There was no disgrace to belong to one of them. They had big bands. The band on the Virginia minstrels was conducted by, uh, Frank Moreland, the father of Mantaan. And Frank Moreland was a wonderful bandmaster. The band on the Virginia minstrels was conducted by Ayers first. And, uh, uh, then later on by, um, what's his name? He lived in Greenville, South Carolina. Max something. But anyhow, it was another wonderful band. And the band on the Alabama minstrels was conducted in variance by four different men. First, Jeff Smith. Next, me. Next, Charlie Lewis. Next, Edward Howard. And he lives in Washington, D.C. now.
